challenges.question: In ancient Egypt, who typically trained to become a physician?
options: Primarily temple-trained scribes and their apprentices
challenges.fact: Egyptian physicians trained in 'Houses of Life' (Per Ankh) — temple scriptoria attached to major sanctuaries. These institutions trained scribes, priests, and healers together — which is why medical texts were preserved alongside religious texts in temple archives.

challenges.question: Peter Arnett became internationally famous for his live TV coverage of which war?
challenges.fact: Peter Arnett broadcast live from Baghdad for CNN during the Gulf War air campaign on January 17, 1991 — the first time a war had been broadcast live on television. His reports from inside the enemy capital were watched by hundreds of millions worldwide.

challenges.question: What Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph was associated with Peter Arnett's Vietnam War coverage?
options: Raising the Flag at Iwo Jima
challenges.fact: Arnett was present and reporting when Eddie Adams took 'Saigon Execution' (1968) — one of Vietnam's most iconic photographs. Arnett himself won the Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting in 1966 for his Vietnam War coverage for the Associated Press.

challenges.question: Arnett's live Gulf War broadcast was possible because of which technology?
challenges.fact: CNN had a special four-wire telephone line and satellite uplink equipment in Baghdad's Al-Rashid Hotel. While other networks evacuated, Arnett and his CNN colleagues stayed — using this equipment to deliver the first live war coverage in television history.

challenges.question: Peter Arnett is from which country?
challenges.fact: Peter Arnett was born in Riverton, New Zealand in 1934. He began his journalism career in New Zealand before moving to Southeast Asia, where he covered the Vietnam War as a young AP reporter — launching one of journalism's most consequential careers.

challenges.question: What was controversial about Arnett's 1998 CNN interview with Osama bin Laden?
options: It was the first Western TV interview with bin Laden after he declared war on the US
He refused to ask difficult questions
challenges.fact: Arnett conducted CNN's 1997 interview with Osama bin Laden — one of the first Western television interviews after bin Laden issued his declaration of jihad against Americans. The interview was controversial for giving bin Laden a platform, but documented his stated intentions years before 9/11.

challenges.question: War correspondents face which unique ethical challenge?
options: Whether to report facts that might endanger military operations or personnel
Whether to use color or black-and-white photography
How long to stay in one location
challenges.fact: War correspondents constantly navigate between their duty to inform the public and the risk of inadvertently sharing information that endangers lives. Arnett faced this throughout his career — from Vietnam to Baghdad — and was criticized and praised for different reports across five decades.

challenges.question: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne in which year?
challenges.fact: Apple Computer was founded on April 1, 1976 in the Jobs family garage in Los Altos, California. Jobs was 21 years old. Wayne sold his 10% stake for $800 shortly after — a share that would have been worth over $100 billion by 2021.

challenges.question: In 1985, Jobs was forced out of Apple. What did he do next?
options: He founded NeXT Computer and acquired Pixar
He went to work in academia
challenges.fact: Jobs founded NeXT Computer (whose operating system later became the foundation of macOS) and purchased Pixar from George Lucas for $5 million in 1986. Pixar went on to produce Toy Story (1995) and transform animated filmmaking.

challenges.question: The 2007 iPhone launch is famous because Jobs announced it as three devices in one. What were they?
challenges.fact: Jobs said: 'We're announcing three revolutionary products today. The first is a widescreen iPod with touch controls. The second is a revolutionary mobile phone. And the third is a breakthrough internet communications device. These are not three separate devices — this is one device. And we are calling it iPhone.'

challenges.question: After returning to Apple in 1997, Jobs' first major move was to eliminate most of Apple's product lines. Why?
options: Apple was losing money on all products
He wanted to focus — fewer products done brilliantly
challenges.fact: When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company had 350 products and was weeks from bankruptcy. He cut the product line to just 4 items. His philosophy: 'Deciding what not to do is as important as deciding what to do.' The iMac, announced the following year, saved the company.

challenges.question: What is the significance of Apple's 1984 Macintosh commercial?
options: It was the first TV ad for a computer
Directed by Ridley Scott, it aired during the Super Bowl and is considered one of the greatest ads ever
It was banned in most countries
challenges.fact: Directed by Ridley Scott and aired once during Super Bowl XVIII (1984), the '1984' Macintosh commercial depicted Apple as a liberator smashing IBM's Orwellian conformity. It is credited with transforming advertising into a medium for brand mythology.

challenges.question: Jobs was known for his 'reality distortion field.' What did this term mean?
options: His use of virtual reality technology
His charismatic ability to convince people to do what seemed impossible
His practice of lying about product features
His tendency to ignore financial reality
challenges.fact: The 'reality distortion field' was coined by Apple engineer Bud Tribble: Jobs could convince engineers that the impossible was achievable through sheer force of conviction, charm, and willpower — often causing them to actually achieve the impossible. It was part admiration, part alarm.

challenges.question: According to legend, how did Valmiki compose the world's first verse (shloka)?
options: He was inspired by a dream
Grief at seeing a hunter kill a crane caused him to cry out in a metered verse
A god appeared and taught him
challenges.fact: Valmiki is said to have witnessed a hunter kill one of a pair of mating cranes. Overcome with grief for the surviving bird, he spontaneously cried out a curse in a perfectly metered verse — later recognized as the first shloka (Sanskrit verse). He is called 'Adi Kavi' — the First Poet.

challenges.question: The Ramayana tells the story of which prince?
challenges.fact: The Ramayana centers on Prince Rama of Ayodhya — his exile with his wife Sita and brother Lakshmana, Sita's abduction by the demon king Ravana, and Rama's journey to rescue her with the help of Hanuman and an army of monkeys. It remains one of Asia's most beloved epics.

challenges.question: How many verses (shlokas) does the Valmiki Ramayana contain?
challenges.fact: The Valmiki Ramayana contains approximately 24,000 shlokas (verses) organized into seven books (kandas). By comparison, Homer's Iliad has about 15,000 lines. The Ramayana has been translated into over 300 languages and continues to shape South and Southeast Asian cultures.

challenges.question: The character Hanuman in the Ramayana is a:
options: Divine monkey general who helps Rama
challenges.fact: Hanuman is a divine being with the form of a monkey — son of the wind god Vayu, devotee of Rama, and one of Hinduism's most beloved figures. He leaps across the ocean to Lanka, finds Sita, and serves as the epitome of selfless devotion (bhakti).

challenges.question: In which present-day country is the Ramayana epic most likely set?
challenges.fact: The Ramayana is set primarily in the Indian subcontinent — Ayodhya (Uttar Pradesh), the forests of central India, and Lanka (traditionally identified with Sri Lanka). Its geography has made it a defining text for Hindu culture across South and Southeast Asia.

challenges.question: The Ramayana's influence in Southeast Asia is visible today in:
options: Temple reliefs at Angkor Wat and traditional dance forms across the region
challenges.fact: The Ramayana spread through Southeast Asia with Indian cultural influence. Angkor Wat (Cambodia) features Ramayana scenes on its walls; Thailand's Ramakien, Indonesia's Ramayana ballet, and Malaysia's Hikayat Seri Rama are all local versions. Valmiki's story shaped an entire civilization.

challenges.question: How did Catherine the Great come to power in Russia?
options: She was elected by the nobility
She led a coup and deposed her husband, Tsar Peter III
She was the legitimate heir to the throne
She married the previous tsar's heir
challenges.fact: In July 1762, Catherine organized a coup against her husband Tsar Peter III — who was widely seen as weak and pro-Prussian. The Imperial Guard supported her; Peter was arrested and died days later (likely murdered). Catherine ruled Russia for 34 years as Catherine II.

challenges.question: Catherine the Great was born in Germany and came to Russia as a princess. What was her birth name?
challenges.fact: Catherine was born Sophie Friederike Auguste von Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729 in Stettin (now Poland). She converted to Russian Orthodoxy and took the name Yekaterina (Catherine) when she married the future Peter III. She was entirely self-made as a Russian ruler.

challenges.question: Under Catherine the Great, Russia's territory expanded significantly in which directions?
options: North into Scandinavia and west into France
South toward the Black Sea and west into Poland and Lithuania
East into China and south into India
North into the Arctic and east into Alaska
challenges.fact: Catherine expanded Russia southward, winning wars against the Ottoman Empire and gaining access to the Black Sea (Crimea, 1783). She also participated in the partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, 1795), adding vast territories. Russia became a major European power under her rule.

challenges.question: Catherine corresponded with Voltaire, Diderot, and d'Alembert. What intellectual movement was she associated with?
challenges.fact: Catherine styled herself as an 'Enlightened Despot' — a ruler who applied Enlightenment rationalism to governance. She exchanged hundreds of letters with Voltaire, invited Diderot to St. Petersburg, and founded the Hermitage Museum. But her liberal reforms were often limited in practice.

challenges.question: Catherine founded the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, now one of the world's greatest art collections. What sparked its creation?
options: Her personal art collection, purchased from European dealers
challenges.fact: Catherine was a voracious art collector, purchasing entire private collections from European dealers and nobility. Her personal collection grew to over 4,000 paintings. What began as private apartments became the Hermitage — now housing over 3 million items.

challenges.question: Despite her Enlightenment ideals, Catherine's reign saw a major peasant uprising. Who led it?
challenges.fact: The Pugachev Rebellion (1773–1775) was the largest peasant revolt in Russian history — led by Yemelyan Pugachev, a Cossack who claimed to be Tsar Peter III. Catherine crushed it brutally. The rebellion revealed the gap between her Enlightenment ideals and Russia's feudal reality.
